Mozart's piano concertos. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed twenty-seven numbered piano concertos between 1767 and 1791, creating what is widely regarded as one of the greatest bodies of work in the concerto genre. Mozart established the Classical concerto structure as a dramatic dialogue between the soloist and the orchestra, moving away from simple soloist accompaniment. He composed most of these works to perform himself at his subscription concerts in Vienna. However, his first four concertos are actually childhood arrangements of keyboard movements by other composers, such as C.P.E. Bach, meaning only twenty-three are entirely original.

Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major is celebrated for its lyrical, dreamlike second-movement Andante, which became globally famous after its use in the 1967 Swedish film Elvira Madigan. In contrast, Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor is the first of only two minor-key concertos Mozart wrote. It is a highly dramatic and turbulent work that was a favorite of Ludwig van Beethoven, who wrote the most frequently performed cadenzas for its outer movements.

The other minor-key concerto is Piano Concerto No. 24 in C minor, featuring the largest orchestra of any of his concertos. Upon hearing it, Beethoven reportedly remarked to a colleague that they would never be able to compose anything so grand.

Piano Concerto No. 9 in E-flat major is nicknamed the Jeunehomme, properly written as Jenamy, after the French virtuoso Victoire Jenamy. It was a breakthrough work in which the piano boldly enters in the second measure of the piece, defying the classical convention of a long opening orchestral exposition.

The chronological numbering system for Mozart's works is the Köchel catalog, created by botanist and mineralogist Ludwig von Köchel. Beethoven's own piano concertos, particularly the third in C minor, were heavily modeled on Mozart's works, showing how profoundly these concertos influenced the course of Classical and Romantic music.
